items.title: CVE-2026-115806 — The Prime Mover – Backup and Migration plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object In…
items.body:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-115806 (score CVSS 9.8).

The Prime Mover – Backup and Migration plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in all versions up to, and including, 2.2.1 via deserialization of untrusted input in the migration search-and-replace routine (recursiveUnserializeReplace()). An unauthenticated attacker can store a crafted, base64-encoded serialized object in wp_comments.comment_content through the standard comment-submission endpoint (wp-comments-post.php).
items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-115806 (score CVSS 9.8).

The Prime Mover – Backup and Migration plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in all versions up to, and including, 2.2.1 via deserialization of untrusted input in the migration search-and-replace routine (recursiveUnserializeReplace()). An unauthenticated attacker can store a crafted, base64-encoded serialized object in wp_comments.comment_content through the standard comment-submission endpoint (wp-comments-post.php). When an administrator subsequently performs a routine Prime Mover export or restore, the plugin base64-decodes that stored value and passes it to unserialize() with no allowed_classes restriction. A Property-Oriented Programming (POP) chain is present in the plugin's own bundled Freemius library (FS_Clone_Manager::__set → FS_Option_Manager::set_option → store() → update_option()), so no additional plugin or theme is required — the plugin ships the gadget itself.

Score CVSS : 9.8

Type de faiblesse (CWE) : CWE-502

items.body:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2021-48016 (score CVSS 9.8).

DedeCMS through 5.8.1-beta contains a PHP code injection vulnerability in ShowMsg() where the HTTP Referer header is written into a DedeTemplate string and included. Unauthenticated attackers can send a crafted Referer to /plus/flink.php?dopost=save with an empty validate code to execute arbitrary PHP and system commands. Exploitation evidence was first observed by the Shadowserver Foundation on 2023-10-14.

Des captures transmises à Cyberattaque.org montrent également ce qui est présenté comme un accès à un compte disposant de privilèges d’administration.

Les personnes à l’origine de la découverte, dont les captures portent la signature LunarisSec , affirment avoir identifié plusieurs failles distinctes : une inclusion de fichier local, une vulnérabilité XSS persistante, des fichiers SQL exposés et, sur un autre service lié à la FSU, une injection SQL.

L’un des éléments transmis à Cyberattaque.org montre l’exploitation présumée d’une faille de type Local File Inclusion, ou LFI . items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par CISA Advisories.

CISA, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre), and partners are releasing joint guidance, Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience , to help organizations understand and manage token usage in support of operations. As organizations adopt third-party super intelligence (SI) services, token-based usage models can affect cost, performance, and access to critical services. Unmanaged token consumption may contribute to rising and unpredictable costs, reduced service availability, degraded performance, token exhaustion, and denial-of-tokens or denial-of-wallet attacks. The guidance outlines practical steps organizations can take to prioritize token allocation, design efficient workflows, improve user prompting practices, leverage caching and reusable context, optimize data before submission, and monitor token consumption over time. Critical infrastructure owners and operators can use this guidance to identify mission-critical functions that depend on SI, understand service provider and operational dependencies, and plan for reduced SI availability during outages, incidents, or periods of high demand. Cyber defenders can also use the guidance to manage SI-enabled cyber defense workflows while maintaining human oversight, governance, and strong cybersecurity fundamentals.

Cybersecurity policy has long treated data protection as a systems problem: encrypt the database, secure the network, restrict access, monitor activity, and keep attackers out. All of that still matters. But those defenses have a major blind spot. Once inside the wall the data itself is at risk. Every time data is used, copied, or moved, the risk that a malicious actor will steal and expose the data significantly increases. Policymakers need to consider a tested method that reduces the value of sensitive information if it compromised. Hospitals, banks, defense contractors and government agencies cannot operate on permanently unreadable data. They need to process records, share information, analyze intelligence and prepare data for artificial intelligence models. The reality is data moves. It travels through cloud platforms, vendors, backups, analytics tools, payment processors, software services, AI pipelines, and partner systems. items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

Late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter of Crime Stoppers broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.

A Toronto crime prevention program that long promised witnesses a safe space to anonymously report tips froze its operations late Wednesday night, hours after a Canadian news outlet reported that more than 1.5 million tips from Crime Stoppers chapters across the country were exposed in a data breach.

Crime Stoppers urges people not to provide their names when submitting information, but reporters at Canada’s CBC broadcaster were able to reach more than a dozen tipsters by reviewing the hacked data made available to them in March by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets).

About half of the 1.5 million leaked tips CBC studied — some dating back 25 years — contained personal information, the outlet reported.

While Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and individual chapters, including Toronto’s, had confirmed the breach in the days after the hack, they offered no detail about what was exposed, blaming the lack of information on vendor Navigate360 and its subsidiary, P3 Global Intel.

But late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.

“Since 1984, people in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous,” Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said in a statement . “This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry.”

Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Register.

Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure. The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running. According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology. The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause. Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. items.title: LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets
items.body:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Register.

Unknown crims compromised LiteLLM's release process on Wednesday, distributing a malicious version (1.107.0) containing malware designed to steal cloud and AI credentials and a remote access trojan (RAT) capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines through PyPI and Docker registries.
items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Register.

Unknown crims compromised LiteLLM's release process on Wednesday, distributing a malicious version (1.107.0) containing malware designed to steal cloud and AI credentials and a remote access trojan (RAT) capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines through PyPI and Docker registries. PyPI quarantined the trojanized version of the popular open source AI gateway within hours, and the Docker image (litellm/litellm:1.107.0) was removed from both Docker Hub and GHCR soon after - but anyone who ran the compromised package on any platform should assume their secrets have been stolen. “Check for /tmp/.pc_once_* (the exfil has already fired if this file exists) and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock (the C2 daemon ran or is still running if this file exists),” advised Aikido Security malware hunter Ilyas Makari. “The same applies to anyone who ran the official Docker image litellm/litellm:1.107.0, or pulled it via the latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags.” The most recent safe version is v1.106.2. Il présente les données comme des « utilisateurs » provenant notamment de France, d’Espagne, d’Allemagne, d’Italie ou encore du Royaume-Uni.

Mais l’unique échantillon publié avec la revendication raconte pour l’instant une histoire très différente : il ne contient aucune donnée d’utilisateur mais la fiche d’un footballeur professionnel , avec des informations sportives déjà publiques.

La ligne diffusée contient notamment le nom du joueur, sa date de naissance, son âge, sa nationalité, son poste, son club et son championnat . Elle comporte également une photographie et plusieurs identifiants techniques.

Un élément est particulièrement révélateur : l’URL de la photo pointe vers media.api-sports.io , un service fournissant des données structurées sur les joueurs, équipes et compétitions de football.

Le champ api_player_id présent dans l’enregistrement renforce cette analyse. Tout indique donc que l’exemple publié provient d’une table utilisée par FootballMinigames pour alimenter ses jeux avec des informations sur les footballeurs.

L’échantillon ne contient ni adresse email, ni mot de passe, ni pseudonyme de joueur du site, ni historique de connexion .

Attaque Mis à jour le 26 octobre 2026 à 5h42 Mairie de Touget : un hacker prend le contrôle du site et y affiche un message anti-Macron Le site internet de la mairie de Touget a été compromis et sa page d’accueil remplacée par un message politique visant Emmanuel Macron. La capture consultée par Cyberattaque.org montre un defacement signé par un acteur utilisant le pseudonyme « GaSsPeR » .

Au moment de la compromission, les internautes se rendant sur mairie-touget.fr ne retrouvaient plus le contenu habituel de la commune mais une page entièrement contrôlée par l’attaquant.

Le pirate a modifié l’apparence du site pour afficher une composition représentant Emmanuel Macron accompagnée de plusieurs messages politiques hostiles au président de la République.

La page porte également la signature « Hacked by GaSsPeR » . Cyberattaque.org ne reprend pas les affirmations politiques affichées par l’attaquant comme des informations factuelles : elles constituent le contenu du defacement et non une communication de la mairie.

Un defacement de ce type montre qu’un tiers est parvenu à modifier les fichiers ou le contenu servi par le site internet . Plusieurs scénarios techniques peuvent conduire à cette situation : compromission d’un compte administrateur, vulnérabilité dans le CMS, faille sur le serveur ou accès détourné chez un prestataire.

La capture disponible ne permet cependant pas de déterminer lequel de ces scénarios a été utilisé.

Attaque Mis à jour le 24 octobre 2026 à 10h53 ENGIE confirme une cyberattaque : des données de ses clients en fuite ENGIE informe de nouveaux clients d’un incident de sécurité ayant touché un outil utilisé par certains de ses partenaires pour commercialiser des offres d’énergie. Des accès non autorisés ont permis de consulter des informations directement liées aux contrats d’électricité ou de gaz, dont les numéros PDL ou PCE et les numéros de contrat .

Dans un email dont Cyberattaque.org s’est procuré une copie, ENGIE confirme qu’un « acte de cyber-malveillance » a récemment affecté cet outil commercial. Le fournisseur ne précise pour le moment ni le nom de la plateforme compromise, ni le partenaire concerné, ni le nombre de clients touchés.

Le périmètre communiqué comprend le nom, le prénom, l’adresse postale, l’adresse email et le numéro de téléphone du client.

S’y ajoutent des données directement rattachées à la fourniture d’énergie : le Point de Livraison (PDL) pour l’électricité ou le Point de Comptage et d’Estimation (PCE) pour le gaz, l’identifiant client ainsi que le numéro de contrat .

ENGIE précise en revanche que les informations bancaires ne sont pas concernées .

Le PDL est un identifiant unique de 14 chiffres permettant d’identifier précisément un point de fourniture électrique. Son équivalent pour le gaz est le PCE. Ces références sont notamment demandées lors de la souscription d’un contrat ou d’un changement de fournisseur.

Signal de veille — The Record.

In an era of hybrid threats, the British government wants to update the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, which carries a maximum fine of £1,000 and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.

The British government proposed on Thursday introducing prison sentences of up to 14 years and unlimited fines for damaging undersea cables and pipelines.

It comes amid growing concerns over the vulnerability of subsea cables to so-called “hybrid warfare” by hostile states, including physical and cyberattacks targeting the cables themselves or the installations and digital systems on land.

According to the consultation’s white paper , the new criminal offenses would cover telecommunications cables, electricity interconnectors and pipelines carrying 99% of the U.K.’s international data traffic and supplying 74% of its gas.

The proposals would replace the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, a Victorian-era law that carries a maximum fine of £1,000 — a fraction of the repair costs — and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.

Under the new proposed law, alongside the 14 years for those found guilty of deliberate damage, perpetrators of reckless damage would face up to 10 years in prison and those of gross negligence up to two years.

The government said it plans to introduce statutory security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications operators, with powers to direct cable and repair providers on national security grounds. Separate rules would govern fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but could expose sensitive information.

Signal de veille — The Record.

The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market.”

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Thursday said it won’t let devices made with surveillance chips manufactured by a Chinese tech firm enter the U.S. market, the first instance of such a ban following the agency’s implementation of tough new rules.

The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC said .

New rules took effect on October 13 that bans devices containing smart components made by companies on a so-called covered list, an official public directory the agency maintains under a 2019 regulation identifying video surveillance, communications and general technology products believed to threaten national security. HiSilicon was included on the list.

Before the new regulations were implemented, agency rules did not ban “otherwise lawful devices” from including component parts manufactured by covered list entities, the press release said.

“The FCC will continue to act with vigilance in protecting and promoting America’s national security,” Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that called the products potential spyware. “Video devices containing surveillance chips produced by Covered List entities pose an obvious and unacceptable risk to the nation and our people.”

The AI Paradox There is a paradox: AI companies exist to extract intelligence from data, yet many have almost no visibility into how their own software is being used. Signal de veille — The Register.

Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans, officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates.
